title: Does the Heaven and Hell System Seem Unfair?
excerpt: Why do some people do good things, while others do bad things?
content:
If we never chose our beginning, how responsible are we for our ending?

Why do some people do good things, while others do bad things?

Sometimes, the way we act and the decisions we make are driven by our emotions. We all have different pasts, different traumas, and different kinds of happiness. Do we really do good things because we are generally happy, and do bad things because we are living with untreated trauma? The reality is more complicated than that.

A study in Frontiers in Psychology found that positive emotional affect was associated with more prosocial behavior in children. It shows that emotionally healthier people are, on average, more cooperative and socially beneficial.

Fortunately and unfortunately, emotions do not always come from ourselves alone. Maybe we have heard the question, “What makes you happy?” but we often forget these important questions: “How did you become happy?” and “How did you become traumatized?” Being loved or being abused are things we cannot choose. Obviously, we all want to be loved. But what if reality gives us the opposite?

So, in this article, I want to tell my story about the time I met a prostitute.

She was 22 years old. She had a smile on her face, though I could still see sadness behind it. It all started because of a stupid prank by my friends. They ordered a prostitute to my place without my knowledge. Back then, I was not really interested in sex. Instead, I asked her to go driving around the city with me. During college, I really liked learning about human behavior, so my objective was simply to understand her point of view. Why did she choose this path?

About her background, she never actually finished high school because she had to leave home and start selling food to raise her younger sisters. She was abused by her father and also sexually assaulted. Her father was an online gambler who ended up broke, selling important belongings, while her mother was constantly beaten by him. Unfortunately, her mother later died from cancer.

She experienced living on the streets for days. The incident was eventually heard by her uncle, her mother’s brother. What a kind-hearted man. He decided to take care of her and her sisters. Her uncle lived alone in a small house and had never been married. It is regrettable that her uncle died in a car crash shortly after deciding to take care of them. He was the only sibling her mother had. What a tragic and unlucky incident.

At least, he left behind a small house, a bag of cash, and a debit card, although there were still debts attached to it. With the little money she had left, she started a small food business for lunch and dinner. At first, things went well. She could afford to send her sisters to school, although she had to sacrifice her own education to keep the business running. But eventually, things stopped getting better.

She did not tell me everything that happened in her 20s. I felt bad asking too deeply. What I could assume was that her past trauma never truly left her. Remembering it was like looking at a cracked egg that could never be fixed again. At some point, she decided to become a prostitute. I never really knew the exact reason. Most likely, she simply needed more money.

One day, she had a client who was a stupid bastard of a husband. He ordered her service after arguing with his wife. Ironically, he was also an online gambler, just like her father, and he ended up broke as well. Imagine having to serve a man who reminds you of the same person who destroyed your childhood.

She told me that the wife eventually found out her husband had ordered a prostitute, and somehow she became the one blamed for everything. The whole situation was chaotic and confusing. She never told me how it ended. We stayed silent for a few minutes inside the car. I could see her eyes becoming watery with sadness, and I was too stunned to ask more.

Then it became her turn to ask me a question.

“How is your family?”

“They are doing fine,” I answered. “I love my mother and father. They always take care of me. They are the reason I became who I am now.”

She interrupted me immediately.

“YOU HAVE TO KNOW THIS,” she said. “YOU ARE LUCKY. I DIDN’T CHOOSE THIS LIFE.”

I tried to calm her down. At the right moment, I asked one more question.

“What makes you happy?”

Her answer was simple.

“I don’t know.”

I did not expect that answer. I thought she would say money.

“How about money?” I asked curiously.

She looked down and quietly replied, “Well, money can buy things, but it doesn’t fix my trauma.”

After that, I asked her to have lunch with me. The food was delicious. Instead of talking about painful things, we decided to tell each other funny stories instead. When we finished, I drove her back home. Her house was simple, shaped almost like a small cube.

On my way back to my place, I cried.

There were too many things inside my mind at once. Gratitude and sadness mixed together. I was grateful to have parents who truly took care of me, but at the same time I kept asking myself: If I were in her position, would I have done the same thing?

People often say that many roads lead to Rome. But we already know not all roads look the same. Some roads are smooth and well-maintained, while others are broken and full of holes. And after choosing one road, we cannot go back and try the others.

So the question becomes: do we really have a choice? Do we truly have free will when, since childhood, our character has already been shaped by our parents, our environment, and our experiences?

Finally, I want to talk about deeds and sins.

Many religious people say we should do good deeds to gain rewards and avoid sins at all costs. But reality is not always that simple. Sometimes, committing sins is not about wanting to destroy society or hurt other people. Sometimes people are simply left with very few choices.

We did not choose to be born into this world. We could not choose our parents. We could not choose whether we would be loved or abused. The only thing we can choose is whether to do good or bad things. But even then, the choices we make are deeply connected to the things we never chose in the first place.

So, does the heaven and hell system seem unfair?
author: Aryachenko

title: Socrates Trend in TikTok Makes Me A Little Concerned
excerpt: In this era of social media, our younger generation receives information easily from these platforms. The short videos we constantly consume are not always beneficial. They can contain misinformation, provocation, and ev
content:
Socrates didn’t start his question because of meaningless confusion

In this era of social media, our younger generation receives information easily from these platforms. The short videos we constantly consume are not always beneficial. They can contain misinformation, provocation, and even false knowledge that gradually leads to ignorance.

And yes, what we see right now is an AI parody video of a skeleton man meeting Socrates. This skeleton character acts annoyed, portraying Socrates as someone who asks too many unnecessary questions. As someone who appreciates philosophy, I admire Socrates as its founding father. Because questioning itself is the peak of knowledge; without the courage to ask, we wouldn’t have the innovations we enjoy today.

Your phone, the internet, electricity, and countless other inventions exist because humans kept asking questions. We have always questioned how to make the world more livable for us. In many ways, we shape our world through curiosity. And it all begins with a question.

When I was a child, I was afraid to ask simple questions to my parents. One day, I asked something I thought was important: “Mom, what would happen if you died tomorrow?” I didn’t mean to offend her. But she was furious. “Why would you ask something like that?” she said. I was scared and couldn’t explain myself. I only wanted to hear her thoughts about death.

For the younger generation, there should be no such thing as a stupid question. Asking is one of the most essential things we do as human beings. Even if a question is wrong, it can always be corrected.

In theory, there are three types of wrong questions. The first is a false premise question — a question based on an incorrect assumption. For example, “How do our lungs produce feces?” We know lungs don’t produce feces; they process oxygen.

The second is a loaded question — a trap designed so that any answer leads to guilt. For instance, “Have you stopped hitting your wife?” Whether you answer yes or no, you are still framed as guilty.

The third is a category error — asking something in the wrong category. Like, “What does a movie taste like?” A movie is something you watch, not something you eat.

In reality, I have never heard anyone, not even children, ask such questions. Most children ask genuine questions — about things they’ve never seen before and want to understand.

When children ask questions that even parents cannot answer, especially in religious families, parents sometimes take a shortcut: “God created all of this” or “It is the beauty of the Creator.” Is this approach wrong? Not entirely. There are both positive and negative sides.

Psychologically, it can comfort the child. They feel satisfied, even if the answer is incomplete. But on the other hand, it may limit their curiosity. If every question leads to the same answer, children may stop asking about the natural world. Their curiosity slowly fades, along with their imagination.

Socrates, who lived 2,500 years ago, asked questions no one had dared to ask before. People could not answer him properly, often relying only on myths and assumptions. Because of his bold questioning, authorities accused him of corrupting beliefs and sentenced him to death. He drank poison, but his questions survived.

This is just my personal opinion, but in today’s TikTok trends, Socrates is portrayed as a foolish man asking nonsense. But that is a misunderstanding. He lived in a world without a fixed system, while we live in one full of established structures.

For example, in one video, Socrates asks, “Why is the maximum rating 5? Why not 67?” This completely misses the point of how Socratic questioning works.

A more accurate analogy, especially in his time, would be something like this:
Imagine Socrates asking, “Why do we believe a king has divine authority? Who decides that one man is chosen by the gods?”

In his era, that question would challenge the very foundation of society. It is not about random numbers, but about questioning assumptions people blindly accept.

The TikTok version turns deep philosophical inquiry into shallow absurdity. It replaces meaningful questioning with meaningless confusion.

Reflection

Questioning is not stupidity. It is the beginning of understanding. The problem today is not that people ask too many questions, but that they ask too few meaningful ones.

In a world flooded with fast content, we are slowly losing the patience to think deeply. We laugh at questions instead of exploring them. We consume answers without ever questioning their origin.

Socrates was not annoying because he asked too much. He was dangerous because he asked the right questions.

Maybe the real issue is not the questions themselves, but our discomfort in facing them.
author: Aryachenko

title: Cyrus the Great: The Man Who Built Not Only Power, but Also Morality
excerpt: In the ancient Near East, political life was shaped by conditions of extreme insecurity. Communities organized themselves along lines of kinship and region, and interactions with outsiders carried the ever-present risk o
content:
The man who has the most power brings morality

The World Before Empires

In the ancient Near East, political life was shaped by conditions of extreme insecurity. Communities organized themselves along lines of kinship and region, and interactions with outsiders carried the ever-present risk of violence. Travel across unfamiliar territories required armed escort, and encounters with people of different languages or appearances were more likely to produce conflict than cooperation. This was not simply a matter of prejudice. It reflected the structural reality of a world where institutions capable of enforcing peace between strangers did not yet exist.

It is against this backdrop that the rise of Cyrus II of Persia, commonly known as Cyrus the Great, must be understood. What distinguished Cyrus from other conquerors of the ancient world was not merely the scale of his military success, but the administrative and ideological framework he constructed to sustain what he had won.

The Achaemenid Expansion

Around 550 BC, Cyrus launched a revolt against the Median Kingdom under Astyages, his maternal grandfather and overlord. The rebellion succeeded, and Cyrus absorbed the Median Empire into what would become the Achaemenid Persian Empire. He subsequently defeated Croesus of Lydia, whose kingdom had long been considered one of the wealthiest in the known world. By 539 BC, his forces stood at the gates of Babylon, the most powerful city in Mesopotamia.

The fall of Babylon is one of the more studied episodes in ancient military history, partly because it occurred with so little of the destruction that typically accompanied conquest in that era. Herodotus recorded that Persian engineers redirected the Euphrates River, lowering the water level beneath the city walls and allowing troops to enter through the riverbed under cover of darkness. More significant than the method of entry, however, was what followed.

Babylon was governed at the time by Nabonidus, a king whose reign had generated considerable internal opposition. He had spent extended periods away from the capital and had neglected the cult of Marduk, the principal deity of the Babylonian religious establishment. This estrangement from both the priesthood and the population created a political vacuum that Cyrus was strategically positioned to fill. Multiple ancient sources, including Babylonian administrative records, indicate that the city fell with minimal resistance and that the existing civil administration was largely left intact. Daily commerce and religious practice continued without significant interruption.

The Cyrus Cylinder: Document and Debate

The most discussed artifact from this period is the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay barrel inscription discovered in 1879 in the ruins of Babylon and now housed at the British Museum. The cylinder, written in Akkadian cuneiform, presents a first-person narrative attributed to Cyrus. It opens by condemning Nabonidus for his neglect of Marduk, describes Cyrus as the chosen instrument of the god, and then details a series of acts attributed to the new king: the liberation of captive peoples, the restoration of cult statues to their original cities, and the authorization of displaced communities to return to their homelands.

The cylinder has occupied a contested position in modern scholarship. In 1971, the United Nations translated it into all six official languages and recognized it in connection with debates over early human rights instruments. Advocates of this interpretation argue that the cylinder represents one of the earliest recorded instances of a ruler formally acknowledging the rights of conquered peoples to maintain their religious identities and cultural practices.

Critics of this reading are numerous, and their objections carry considerable weight. Amélie Kuhrt, a leading scholar of Achaemenid history, has argued that the cylinder is best understood within the conventions of Mesopotamian royal inscription rather than as a declaration of universal principle. In the ancient Near East, it was standard practice for incoming rulers to present themselves as restorers of divine order, criticize their predecessors as impious, and enumerate their own acts of clemency. Viewed through this lens, the Cyrus Cylinder is less a founding document of human rights and more a sophisticated piece of political communication directed at a Babylonian audience whose cooperation Cyrus needed.

The scholarly consensus today occupies a middle position. The cylinder almost certainly reflects actual policies. Archaeological and administrative evidence from the Persian period corroborates that Cyrus did permit displaced populations to return home and did allow for the restoration of local religious practices. The Jewish community is a notable example: the Book of Ezra records that Cyrus authorized the return of Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem and permitted the rebuilding of the Temple. This account is broadly consistent with what is known about Persian policy toward subject peoples more generally.

What the cylinder does not represent, most historians agree, is a statement of universal rights in the modern sense. The protections it describes were not extended to all peoples under Persian rule as a matter of legal principle. They were applied strategically, in contexts where winning the goodwill of local elites and religious establishments served the interests of imperial governance.

Governance as a Political Technology

The more analytically productive framing may be to understand Cyrus not primarily as a humanitarian, but as an exceptionally effective administrator who recognized that a sustainable empire required something beyond military force. The Persian model of rule, developed under Cyrus and refined by his successors Cambyses and Darius I, was organized around tolerance not as a moral ideal but as an instrument of control.

Conquered peoples who were permitted to retain their languages, gods, and customs had fewer reasons to resist Persian authority. Local elites who were incorporated into the administrative structure had material incentives to cooperate. Religious establishments that received Persian patronage became, in effect, stakeholders in the stability of the empire. This approach stood in marked contrast to the Assyrian model, which had relied more heavily on mass deportation and the destruction of local institutions as mechanisms for eliminating organized resistance.

The Greek historian Xenophon, writing in the fourth century BC, offered an idealized portrait of Cyrus in the Cyropaedia, a text that is part history and part political philosophy. Xenophon used Cyrus as a vehicle for exploring questions about leadership, education, and the qualities required of a good ruler. The portrait is openly admiring and should be read with some critical distance. Xenophon was not simply recording history. He was constructing an argument about governance. Nevertheless, the persistence of Cyrus as a model of enlightened rulership across Greek, Jewish, and later Western traditions suggests that his approach to empire made a lasting impression on those who encountered or studied it.

Historical Significance

The legacy of Cyrus the Great cannot be reduced to either uncritical admiration or cynical dismissal. The evidence supports a reading in which pragmatic imperial calculation and genuinely tolerant policy coexisted without contradiction. Cyrus governed an empire that stretched from the Aegean coast to the borders of the Indian subcontinent, encompassing dozens of languages, religions, and legal traditions. Maintaining that empire required strategies that could accommodate diversity rather than eliminate it.

Whether this constitutes an anticipation of modern human rights norms is a question that historians continue to debate. The anachronism of applying contemporary legal concepts to ancient political arrangements is a real methodological risk. What can be said with more confidence is that Cyrus developed and implemented a model of imperial governance that prioritized the preservation of existing institutions over their destruction, and that this model proved remarkably durable.

The Cyrus Cylinder, whatever its precise ideological function in its original context, has become a significant artifact in the longer history of how power has been justified and contested. It documents an early instance of a ruler feeling compelled to articulate the basis of his legitimacy in terms that extended beyond simple military victory. Power, the inscription implies, requires consent. Governance requires justification. These are not modern ideas. They are very old ones.

References

  • The Cyrus Cylinder and Ancient Persia (2013), https://www.britishmuseum.org/exhibitions/cyrus-cylinder-ancient-persia
  • The Cyrus Cylinder (n.d.), https://www.worldhistory.org/Cyrus_Cylinder/
  • Cyrus the Cylinder Is Not a Charter of Human Rights (2013), https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/mar/11/cyrus-cylinder-not-human-rights-charter
  • Ancient Near Eastern Royal Inscriptions and Propaganda (2005), https://oi.uchicago.edu/research/publications
  • Histories — Herodotus (c. 440 BC), https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Hdt.+1
  • Cyropaedia — Xenophon (c. 370 BC), https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Xen.+Cyrop.
  • Book of Ezra (c. 5th century BC), https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ezra+1

title: We Feared Imagined Problems More Than The Real Ones Before Us
excerpt: In our current era, scientists are able to explain phenomena we can’t see with our bare eyes, like the spread of viruses. We can know the origin of a virus, how to stop its spread, and develop a vaccine. We know what we
content:
When Uncertainty Breeds Confusion and Conflict Within Us

In our current era, scientists are able to explain phenomena we can’t see with our bare eyes, like the spread of viruses. We can know the origin of a virus, how to stop its spread, and develop a vaccine. We know what we should do. But it’s different from what our ancestors had experienced.

Humans have always feared what they cannot see. When disasters came without clear explanations, such as plagues and celestial phenomena like the one that happened in Nuremberg in 1561, humans were terrified of uncertainty. No explanation, no solution came to their minds. People believed that the church leaders were the wise ones. They hoped the church knew how to overcome the disaster.

I’ll start with two stories that show how humans tried to overcome uncertainty, and how chaotic it was. We began with irrational ways before moving toward rational ways to overcome disasters.

The Second Punic War occurred from 218 BC to 201 BC. It was a huge loss for Ancient Rome against Carthage, which was led by Hannibal Barca. He did the unthinkable by crossing the Alps with an army that included war elephants. Rome didn’t expect they would appear from the north because they believed the Alps were a natural shield, so no one would think of crossing them.

It started with the Battle of the Ticinus (218 BC), followed by the Battle of the Trebia (218 BC), the Battle of Lake Trasimene (217 BC), and the Battle of Cannae (216 BC). In the first three years of the invasion of Italy, Rome suffered huge losses, with more than 100,000 casualties. That was a massive number for a relatively small and developing civilization.

The people of Rome went insane thinking that Hannibal would crush the heart of Rome. If that happened, it would be the worst disaster they could imagine. These defeats were not seen merely as military failures, but as signs of divine anger. In response, they performed extraordinary rituals to appease the gods, including the burial of human victims alive.

For example, the Vestal Virgins, who were tasked with maintaining the sacred fire, were punished if they lost their virginity. Those who broke their vow were buried alive, and the men involved were beaten to death, often based on quick accusations.

Such disasters eventually led to real solutions. The Battle of Cannae alone wiped out around 20% of Rome’s army, so they needed to raise new soldiers. They began recruiting slaves and lowering the age requirement for military service. The Romans also realized that Hannibal always won in open-field battles. Therefore, it was unlikely that Hannibal would risk attacking the heavily fortified city of Rome itself.

Scipio Africanus, a Roman general who had studied Hannibal’s tactics carefully, eventually led the Roman army in the Battle of Zama (202 BC). He understood how to neutralize Hannibal’s war elephants. This battle ended in a decisive defeat for Carthage. It became one of the greatest strategic turnarounds in military history.

From this story, we can see how sudden panic led to chaotic confusion. Humans searched for quick explanations. Perhaps the gods were angry, so they believed they needed to appease them. But after the panic settled, people began to gather and say, “Alright, we need to find a real solution.”

The second story is about the deadliest plague in history, once known as the Black Death. Humanity was almost wiped out because of this disease. Doctors at that time did not actually understand how the disease spread. Because of that, people once again turned to the church as the source of wisdom.

Little did they know that the authority of Pope Gregory IX had previously encouraged the killing of cats. Cats were associated with witches and dark magic. The reduction of cat populations may have allowed rats, the carriers of the plague, to multiply even more. Their fear only worsened the real situation.

People believed the plague had been sent as a curse from God. What they didn’t realize was that one of the factors that worsened the spread of the disease came from an order they believed was “an order from God.”

That sounds silly to our ears today. But remember, humans fear uncertainty. That doesn’t mean they were stupider than we are today. Eventually, they also came up with real solutions. Early quarantine practices were introduced, and societies gradually developed better sanitation, urban management, and disease control.

Reflection

Sometimes I think we live in the perfect era. Many questions have already been answered. Piece by piece, the puzzle has been solved. We no longer look for solutions based purely on uncertain beliefs. When I get sick, the chaotic panic that humans once experienced is no longer there. Medication provided by doctors today is the real solution to many of our illnesses.

Even today, however, many people still die from diseases that are difficult to cure, such as cancer. When someone is diagnosed with cancer, many people assume it means there is no hope left. But remember, our bodies are not as weak as we might think.

Maybe we no longer need to believe in the old dogmas of the past, but we can still keep the positive mindset humans once relied on. If you believe in yourself and believe that you can recover, your body will do its best to fight the cancer cells.

So in a way, humanity has moved from believing in dogma to believing in something else: “yourself”.
author: Aryachenko

title: Would I Worship Ra, the God of the Sun, If I Had Been Born in Ancient Egypt?
excerpt: This question reveals something fundamental about human nature. The gods humans worship have changed countless times throughout history, shaped by geography, culture, and era. But behind those shifting beliefs lies somet
content:
This question reveals something fundamental about human nature. The gods humans worship have changed countless times throughout history, shaped by geography, culture, and era. But behind those shifting beliefs lies something constant about how humans understand the meaning of life.

Let me tell you the story behind Egyptian mythology, one of the oldest belief systems humanity has ever had. Their highest god is Ra, the God of the Sun. He created the world by creating other gods. From myths, rituals, and religious texts, Egyptian priests interpreted the duties of humans toward Ra.

The meaning of life, in their belief, is related to the concept of cosmic balance called Ma’at. Ma’at is not just a moral rule, but the order of the universe: righteousness, justice, harmony, and regularity that keep the world on its path. What people were supposed to do was live truthfully, never steal, never deceive, respect the gods, and maintain social balance.

I find it intriguing that humans deeply care about trusting one another. Never stealing, never lying, and maintaining social balance are moral principles that help build a great civilization. As we know, developed ancient civilizations were never separate from their religions. There were many questions without answers about how the world actually works. Humans were amazed and tried to find answers or sometimes create them.

Before the Renaissance era, humans tended to create answers rather than discover them. People did not have the technology we have today to investigate reality. Religious texts therefore came in handy to satisfy human curiosity. For hundreds of years, it worked. People lived in relative peace, solved many problems, and learned how to survive in this world. These religious practices still exist today. Some people worship God because it brings them calm. Or perhaps it is one of their mandatory activities to communicate with God, hoping they will find solutions to their problems.

I believe in monotheism, but I won’t say which religion. The point is that I believe in one God who created this universe. And of course, this idea is different from Ra, because Ra was born from a place called Nun, a chaotic primordial sea. This leads to another question for people today: who created Nun? In monotheistic belief, God exists before space and time themselves. As simply put: God created everything. But another question comes to my mind.

What if I had been born in Ancient Egypt? Would I worship their gods, or would I stand against them?

Here is the thing: if I had been born there, I would have lived in an era when humanity had very few answers to the puzzles of the universe. I would not know that there are other suns in other solar systems. I would not know that the sun does not actually move up and down to create day and night, while our Earth is the one rotating.

Besides amazement, humans also feel fear when faced with many unanswered questions. I could not expect myself to be like Socrates in that era. There would be an inner conflict if someone decided to abandon the common belief, just as Socrates once challenged the beliefs of his society.

What if the gods actually existed? Would Osiris punish me for what I had done and send me to the monster called Ammit to be eaten? Does fear work like a chain, or does it provide comfort?

Would I be the person who stands before everyone and says, “Yes, you are all wrong”? What boldness that would require. In the next minute, the authorities might arrest you and execute you. So such bravery would be almost impossible. Humans tend to find ways to survive rather than pursue truth itself.

I cannot accept the idea, based on my current thinking, that I would worship Ra if I had been born there. But there is no guarantee that my way of thinking would be the same. It would most likely be very different from who I am today. I would simply live my daily life, respect the Pharaoh, and pray to the gods. What makes me who I am today is what exists in my mind now.

Reflection

Survival is the first priority we tend to choose. Life might have an absurd meaning, but what of it? Are we going to accept that and live like a disaster?

No matter how you interpret the meaning of life, as long as it gives you the urge to stay alive and continue doing what you love, perhaps that is already enough.
author: Aryachenko

title: Why Humans Are Never Truly Satisfied and Why It’s Good
excerpt: Human beings are never truly satisfied. When someone does not have a vehicle, he envies those who do. Those who have a vehicle envy someone who owns a sports car. And when a person finally owns the most expensive car in
content:
Human beings are never truly satisfied. When someone does not have a vehicle, he envies those who do. Those who have a vehicle envy someone who owns a sports car. And when a person finally owns the most expensive car in the world and is the only one who has it, will he be satisfied? At the beginning, perhaps yes. But eventually, he will want more. Maybe he will expand his collection, or maybe he will try to create something even more expensive than the most expensive. It seems that humans are greedy creatures. A trait that is often considered sinful and disliked by God. But before we judge it too quickly, we need to understand our greed more deeply. Does greed bring progress or destruction to the world? Is it a defect or a strength?

To explore this question, let us travel far back, around 300000 years ago, to the beginning of our existence. At that time, what were we capable of? We could make fire, craft weapons for hunting, and create simple clothing. Our primary concern was survival. Getting food was exhausting, dangerous, and often deadly. People back then were not thinking about entertainment, technology, music, the internet, production machines, or even proper housing. Their problem was simple and brutal. How do we eat tomorrow?

The only solutions they could imagine were solutions related to survival. Then, about 10000 years ago in the Neolithic era, humans discovered agriculture and domestication. Food became more stable and predictable. Life, at least in terms of survival, became easier. But did humans become satisfied? Clearly not. The solution they discovered created new problems. The concept of ownership emerged. This is mine, that is yours, let us exchange. Barter did not always work smoothly. Crime appeared. Theft and murder became alternatives for those who wanted something without paying the price. As conflicts increased, humans needed rules. Laws were created to protect rights and punish wrongdoing. Leaders and law enforcers emerged. Early civilizations such as Mesopotamia and Egypt flourished. Humans organized themselves under systems, accumulated wealth, and began searching for deeper answers about the world.

As civilization expanded, mobility became crucial. At first, horses were the primary means of transportation. But horses required food and had physical limitations. Humans then improved the wheel and transportation systems, allowing movement across regions. Exploration began. Humans became curious. Humans observed. Humans desired. This cycle repeated itself through centuries of expansion, from Cyrus the Great to Alexander the Great, from Julius Caesar to Genghis Khan, and later to Adolf Hitler. Many argue that war shaped civilization. But perhaps war was not the true engine of progress. Perhaps the deeper engine was human greed. Not merely the desire for domination, but also the desire to know more.

From that point, curiosity began to shape a different path. During the Renaissance and the Age of Enlightenment, humans started questioning mythological explanations that lacked empirical evidence. Instead of inventing stories, they began conducting observations. Figures like Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton, Nikola Tesla, and Albert Einstein changed the trajectory of knowledge. Steam engines, telephones, airplanes, computers, the internet, and eventually artificial intelligence transformed daily life. Humanity searched for ways to make the Earth more manageable and more compatible with human needs.

If we compare our current condition with the distant past, the difference is astonishing. We no longer need to hunt daily for survival. Information travels instantly. Knowledge is accessible almost everywhere. Many daily tasks have become easier. But has the human problem been solved? Certainly not. Poverty, injustice, greed, and conflicts between nations still exist. Our curiosity has not stopped. In fact, the complexity of our problems has increased. As we try to make the Earth more comfortable for humans, we develop artificial intelligence and android robotics to assist us. We want faster results. When newspapers first appeared, they were the fastest source of information compared to rumors. Now, AI-powered systems provide information even faster and often more accurately. In the end, humans will always search for something greater than the greatest and faster than the fastest.

The idea that humans are never satisfied usually carries a negative meaning. It is associated with radical ambition for wealth and power. But let us consider a different scenario. What if humans had become satisfied 100000 years ago? What if we were content with hunting as our permanent way of life? To see a possible answer, we can look at one of our evolutionary relatives, Homo erectus. Homo erectus existed for nearly two million years, far longer than Homo sapiens has existed so far. During that time, what did they achieve? Did they develop nuclear technology? Did they travel to the Moon? Did they send sa pacecraft beyond the solar system? For millions of years, their lifestyle remained relatively unchanged. They lived in caves from generation to generation until extinction. Their brains were smaller than ours. Their cognitive capacity was limited compared to Homo sapiens. If curiosity and dissatisfaction had not pushed our species to migrate from Africa to other continents and eventually develop agriculture, perhaps we would have shared the same fate.

greed
[ɡriːd] intense and selfish desire for something

Based on morals, religion, and tradition, greed almost always carries a negative connotation, like in Christianity, where greed is one of the seven deadly sins. However, from a psychological and evolutionary perspective, greed is far more complex than that. This leads me to my own theory about human greed. I divide it into two categories, Radical Greed and Progressive Greed. Radical Greed is the desire to dominate, control, and overpower. It is directed toward personal or national supremacy. This type of greed operates on a zero-sum logic. If I rise, you must fall. It often results in conflict and exploitation. Imperialism, authoritarianism, and the takeover of natural resources are examples. The compass of this greed has two primary directions, fear and insecurity.

In contrast, Progressive Greed focuses on knowledge. It is driven by curiosity and the desire to understand. Instead of conquering people, it seeks to conquer ignorance. This type of greed produces innovation. From the discovery of fire to the rise of early civilizations, from the scientific revolution to quantum physics and artificial intelligence, progress has been fueled by this inner hunger for answers. One greed enslaves others. The other liberates humanity from ignorance.

Reflection

Finally, let us move to a higher perspective. Imagine that all humans who have ever lived are gathered by God from the first generation until the last. Then He asks a simple question. What did you truly want during your life on Earth? Which word would dominate the answers? More? Meaning? Security? Happiness? Power? Success? What do humans actually seek beneath all achievements and conflicts? What have we truly contributed? Is our curiosity merely a biological accident shaped by evolution without deeper meaning? Or is it something more profound that defines what it means to be human?
author: Aryachenko

title: The Policeman Who Hated the Empire He Served
excerpt: The British Empire was the largest empire in history. Discrimination, racism, and exploitation were among the bad behaviors the British Empire used to practice. Many nations freed themselves from such colonialism, either
content:
The British Empire was the largest empire in history. Discrimination, racism, and exploitation were among the bad behaviors the British Empire used to practice. Many nations freed themselves from such colonialism, either by fighting back or through diplomatic ways. There was one Englishman who hated his own nation because of this system. He was George Orwell, known as the legendary writer with his famous works, Animal Farm and 1984.

He served as a British colonial police officer in Burma from 1922–1927. He joined the Indian Imperial Police when he was only 19 years old. That moment became the foundation of his ideas about power, discrimination, and morality.

There were many moments he witnessed that made him start hating imperialism. He wrote about one of them in his essay Shooting an Elephant. He worked in a small city named Moulmein in the 1920s. One morning, he received a report that there was a working elephant in musth condition. The elephant went insane, destroyed kiosks, turned over carts, and people started panicking. When Orwell arrived, the situation had finally eased. The elephant was calmly eating grass in a field.

But the conflict did not end there.

Orwell had a rifle in his hand. He brought it just in case he needed to use it. Thousands of Burmese were watching behind him. They did not bring rifles. They had only one hope: “That Englishman will shoot.”

His mind began to struggle between morality and rationality. The elephant was already calm, so he did not have to kill it. Morally, it would be wrong to shoot it. But socially and politically, he was the symbol of British power. If he chose not to shoot, he would be seen as weak. He would be mocked.

He became more stressed. Many eyes were staring at him. He aimed the rifle and shot the elephant. But the elephant did not die instantly. It staggered and tried to stand again. It moaned in pain and slowly collapsed. Orwell shot it a few more times. The most haunting thing was not a quick death, but the long suffering of the elephant. It took more than 30 minutes to die. Orwell left before the elephant was completely dead because he could not bear to watch it.

In another essay, A Hanging, Orwell tells his experience of witnessing the execution of a Burmese prisoner. As they were walking to the gallows, there was a very small detail. On the road, there was a puddle. The prisoner stepped aside to avoid it so his legs would not get wet.

That moment was like thunder.

Why?

Because it showed something very simple but deeply meaningful. The prisoner still had reflexes, still cared about small comforts, and still responded to the world naturally. He was fully human, and within minutes, his life would be taken deliberately.

After five years, Orwell decided to resign as a British colonial police officer. He was done with the colonial system. He realized he was part of a structural injustice. In 1927, he returned to England. It was a bold decision; he left a promising career to become a writer and lived in poverty.

“Colonizer are also the prisoner of the great power itself”
author: Aryachenko

title: This Is Why I Decided to Learn Russian
excerpt: Hello, my name is Arya Shevchenko. I am from Indonesia, and I am 22 years old. I have been learning Russian for three months. Russian is my third language.
content:
Hello, my name is Arya Shevchenko. I am from Indonesia, and I am 22 years old. I have been learning Russian for three months. Russian is my third language.

Many people ask me, “Why Russian?”

I see Russian as part of my future. I have long been interested in Russian history from the Russian Empire to the Soviet Union and the modern Russian Federation. I am fascinated by its culture, literature, and way of thinking.

I live in a warm country where the weather is always hot. One of my life principles is to experience everything the world has to offer. Russia is one of the coldest countries in the world. For me, it represents not just a place, but a completely different way of life.

I believe Russia is one of the most underrated destinations for pursuing a master’s degree. Many people from my country choose Germany, Japan, Singapore, Australia, or the UK. It is not about being afraid to compete. I simply have a personal connection to Russia that is hard to explain in words. I always choose Russia as my first option.

Yes, Russian is considered one of the hardest languages in the world. But that difficulty attracts me. At 22 years old, I refuse to let my brain stop learning. Learning a new language strengthens memory and improves the ability to recognize patterns in sentence structure. These skills are useful in real life. It is like telling my brain, “No, it’s not time for you to rest.”

I have talked with many Russians on the app HelloTalk. I asked them about life in Saint Petersburg, Moscow, Kazan, and even cities I had never heard of before. Some want to leave Russia, while others want to stay. So I still cannot conclude whether life there is good or bad.

Interestingly, many of them dream of visiting warm countries like Indonesia. I even debated with a Russian woman about which climate is better for humans, four seasons or just dry and rainy seasons.

I told her that I dream of living in a snowy country. Skating, hockey, and snow all look beautiful to me. Maybe that sounds childish. But that childish curiosity is one of the reasons I started learning Russian.

She told me that living in Russia can be very hard. She even shared a news story about a man who died after being hit by falling snow from a roof. Her point was clear: “You will find new problems that your country does not have.”

And she was right.

But that moment did not change my dream. I understand that if I move to Russia for a master’s degree and work, I will face new challenges. But that is exactly the life I want.

My principle is not only to solve my current problems, but to search for new struggles. Humans are naturally curious. I think about the first Homo sapiens who left Africa and migrated to Europe. They did not find an easier life. They faced cold weather and new dangers. They had to adapt. But that adaptation led to human progress.

We discover. We learn.

And that word “learn” is my principle.

I do not want to die before experiencing the greatness this world has to offer.
author: Aryachenko

title: Это почему я решил учусь русский язык
excerpt: Здразвуйте, меня зовут Арья Шевченко. Я из Индонезии. Мне 22 года. Я изучаю русский язык уже три месяца. Русский мой третий язык.
content:
Здразвуйте, меня зовут Арья Шевченко. Я из Индонезии. Мне 22 года. Я изучаю русский язык уже три месяца. Русский мой третий язык.

Многеи люуди спрашивают меня «Почему русский?».

Я вижу русский язык как своё будущее. Меня давно интересует история от Российской Империи до Советского Союза и современной Российсской Федерации. Мне интересны куьтура, литература и мышление русского народа.

Я живу в тёплой стране, где всегда жарко. Один из моих жизненных принципов испытать всё, что может предложить мир. Россия одна из самых холодных стран в мире. Для меня это не только география, но и совершенно другой образ жизни.

Я считаю, что Россия одна из самых недооценённых стран для получения степени магистра. Многие люди из моей выбирают Германию, Японию, Сингапур, Австралию или Великобританию. Дело не в страхе конкуренции. У меня просто есть личный интерес к России, который трудн объяснить словами. Я всегда выбираю Россию как свой первый вариант.

Да, русский язык считается одним из самых сложных языков в мире. Но именно сложность меня привлекает. В 22 года я не хочу, чтобы мой мозг перестал учиться. Изучение нового языка развивает память и помогает видеть закономерности в структуре предложений. Эти навыки полезны и в реальной жизни. Это как будто я говорю своему мозгу: «Нет, ещё не время отдыхать».

Я общался со многими русскими людьми в приложении HelloTalk. Я спрашивал их о жизни в России в Санкт-Петербурге, Москве, Казани и даже городах, о которых раньше никогда не слышал. Некоторые хотят уехать за границу, другие хотят остаться. Поэтому я не могу сделать однозначный вывод, хороша ли жизнь в России или нет.

Интересно, что многие из них хотят посетить тёплые страны, такие как Индонезия. Я даже спорил с одной русской девушкой о том, какой климат лучшее для человека четыре времени года или только сухой и дождливый сезоны.

Я говорил, что мечтаю жить в снежной стране. Мне кажется это красивым: катание на коньках хоккей, снег. Возможно, это звучит по-детски. Но именно эта детская любознательность стала одной из причин, почему я начал учить русский язык.

Та девушка сказала мне, что жить здесь тяжело. Она рассказала случай, когда человек погиб, потому что на него упал снег с крыши. Она сказала «Ты найдёшь новые проблемы, которых нет в твоей стране».

И она права.

Но этот разговор не изменил мою мечту. Я понимаю, что я поеду в Россию учиться и работать, я столкнусь с новыми трудностямию Но именно такую жизнь я и хочу.

Мой принцип не только решать существующие проблемы, но и искать новые вызовы. Человек по природе любознателен. Я думаю о первых Homo Sapiens, которые покинули Африку и отправились в Европу. Они не нашил «лёгкую жизнь». Они столкнулись адаптираваться. Но именно это привело к развитию человечества.

Мы находим новое. Мы учимся.

Именно слово «учиться» это мой принцип.

Я не хочу умереть, не испытав всё великое, что может предложить этот мир.
author: Aryachenko

title: Alan Turing Saved the World, and Few People Know It
excerpt: Alan Turing was known as the father of the modern computer. He introduced a concept called the “Turing Machine,” a theoretical model that became the foundation of all modern computers. Even the concept of algorithms that
content:
Alan Turing was known as the father of the modern computer. He introduced a concept called the “Turing Machine,” a theoretical model that became the foundation of all modern computers. Even the concept of algorithms that we use in machine learning today is rooted in his model.

During World War II at Bletchley Park, Turing and his team decrypted the Nazi Enigma cipher. The Bombe machine that he designed was able to decode Germany’s secret messages. The Nazis relied on Enigma to coordinate submarine attacks, military operations, and strategic movements across Europe. Without breaking that code, the Allies would have been blind to the Nazis’ next targets.

Many historians estimate that this breakthrough shortened the war by at least two years. That is not a short time. In the deadliest war humanity has ever faced, two additional years could have cost millions of lives. In an extreme scenario, if the escalation had continued for two more years — including expanded strategic bombing, mass starvation across Europe and Asia, and the possible use of more weapons of mass destruction — the number of deaths could have reached nearly 12 million per year. Two years would mean around 24 million lives.

He not only contributed to his own time, but also to the future. He asked a question that still echoes today:

“Can machines think?”

His proposed “Imitation Game,” now known as the Turing Test, began as a paper titled “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” It reframed intelligence not as internal consciousness, but as observable behavior. In the age of artificial intelligence, this question feels less philosophical and more immediate.

His model was revolutionary because in 1950, computers were still as large as rooms, and the concept of AI sounded like science fiction. Turing predicted that within decades, machines would be able to fool humans in conversation within minutes. A bold prediction for that era.

He believed that humans follow the laws of physics. If a biological system can produce intelligence, why not a mechanical one? Turing had already begun exploring the question of behaviorism versus consciousness long before deep learning existed.

And yet, in 1952, he was prosecuted by his own country for being homosexual. He was given two choices: prison or chemical castration through hormone therapy. He chose chemical castration.

There are many theories about how he died. Some believe it was suicide by cyanide poisoning. Others suggest alternative explanations. Imagine being someone who helped save countless lives, yet being treated as a criminal by your own country.

A late redemption came in 2013, when Queen Elizabeth II officially granted him a royal pardon. In 2017, the United Kingdom enacted the “Turing Law,” extending pardons to thousands of others who had been punished under the same law.
author: Aryachenko
